fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title":"Six Gold Pages, Huge Claim","body":"The object at the center of this episode sits in the Bulgarian National Museum of History in Sofia: six leaves of what is claimed to be 23.82 karat gold, about five centimeters long, held together by gold rings, and dated to roughly 600 BC. Chance Garton keeps stressing the scale, since the whole thing is shorter than a golf tee and weighs around 100 grams. Dylan Saccoccio reads the letterforms as a mix, including a character that works like an Umbrian ph, which he would not expect that early, though regional variation across early Italian city states keeps him from calling it fake outright."},{"title":"Where The Search Results Die","body":"Type the artifact into Google and the summary calls it widely considered the oldest multi page bound book in the world. Chance clicks through to the sources and finds a post in a Facebook group called Archaeology and Civilizations, plus a journal item in the Brigham Young University Scholars Archive. Dylan notes that his own article, which he says is the only transliteration of the inscription made readable in Latin letters, does not appear in the first three pages of results. Both describe academic journals as gated, which is why they used AI to surface citations they could then verify."},{"title":"Golden Plates And Borrowed Faith","body":"The book is called Orphic because it resembles small gold afterlife leaves, the German totenpass, even though those are rolled into amulets and never bound, and Dylan says nothing in his transliteration points to Orpheus at all. The Brigham Young piece goes further, linking the find to Lehi leaving Jerusalem and to the plates Joseph Smith described. Chance calls this a perfect microcosm of scriptural stories being treated as the history that artifacts get judged against, and Dylan argues that Europe is constantly made to originate in the Orient to prop up those inherited fables."},{"title":"The Director Who Kept Announcing","body":"Nearly every public claim about the book traces back to one man, museum director Bozhidar Dimitrov, who presented it in 2003. Chance found that Vladimir Georgiev, named then as the translator, had died around 1986, some seventeen years before that announcement, and that the experts in Sofia and London who supposedly authenticated the find were never named or their methods documented. In 2010 Dimitrov told the press he had the bones of John the Baptist before any dating was done, which got him shunned by Sofia University and triggered an inquiry that surfaced an earlier career as a communist agent."},{"title":"Cheap Gold, Priceless Headline","body":"The story is that an anonymous 87 year old man found it in a tomb while working on a canal along the Struma River and handed it over decades later, leaving no dig site, sediment layer, or associated finds. No metallurgy has been published, not even basic X-ray fluorescence, and Chance says his emails to the museum in English and Bulgarian went unanswered. He prices the gold at roughly 1,100 dollars in 2003 against an Etruscan bronze that sold at Christie's for nearly 400,000, which is their answer to why anyone would forge in real gold."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Six pages of beaten gold, and one enormous claim: the oldest book in the world. The Golden Orphic Book, a six-page Etruscan gold codex dated to 600 BC, is almost certainly a forgery, and the story of how it was sold to the public is a masterclass in how corrupt archaeology and the dead internet manufacture false history, one Facebook-sourced search result at a time. In this episode we do a complete forensic breakdown of the Golden Etruscan Book, and the reasons the Etruscan language cannot truly be translated. This episode will give you the tools to spot ancient artifact forgery, including a transliteration of the text in the Plus+ Extension.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Why the Looting Market Rewards a Fake", "body": "In late April, 337 looted antiquities held in the United States were returned to Italy, 221 of them traced through New York prosecutors alone, a haul of Roman, Greek, Etruscan and Egyptian objects taken in clandestine digs or stolen outright from museums. Chance and Dylan use the case to sketch the buyer at the far end of that chain, the collector with too much money and a need to own something unique and priceless that nobody else will ever see, and to make a blunter point, that forgeries move far more easily into private hands than past a museum's scrutiny, so the incentive to manufacture one never goes away."}, {"title": "The Cippus Perusinus Overlap", "body": "The exclusive hour turns on a second artifact, a stone stele found on the hill of San Marco in Perugia in 1822, carrying roughly 130 words of Etruscan and ranking as the fourth longest inscription that survives. Wikipedia calls the Golden Book a pastiche of it. Chance fed both texts to an AI and got back a seventy percent perfect match, a twenty percent near match, and only ten percent unique to the book, then spent the hardest work of the whole project checking every claimed match with his own eyes rather than trusting the number he was handed."}, {"title": "A Date Resting on Handwriting Alone", "body": "The Cippus is conventionally dated to 200 BC, and the single load bearing support for that date is paleography, the study of historical handwriting. It was never excavated from a sealed stratum, no soil or rock layers were studied, and no datable grave goods or other objects were found alongside it. Worse, the mainstream story of Etruscan holds that the alphabet lost letters over time, which runs against every better documented writing system, where alphabets gain letters as they evolve. Dylan points to Godfrey Higgins citing scholars who counted the Etruscan alphabet at twelve or thirteen letters."}, {"title": "Reading the Matches Letter by Letter", "body": "Line by line the two texts get laid side by side, and the picture turns messier than any headline percentage. Velthina, Afun, fusle and susle, rasne and tesne, ras aras, falaschi, felic and larthal, and an eight letter run of thilscuna all turn up on both objects. Some are exact, some differ by a single glyph that may be a copyist flipping an L into a P, and some are just common words in a shared language. Thaura and helu, read as an erected tomb, tie the tower to the grave and connect back to their earlier work on Taurus."}, {"title": "The Verdict and the Cost of Being Wrong", "body": "Reckoning the odds like a poker player, Chance lands on forgery. The Dimitrov problem, the anonymous donor and broken provenance, a suspiciously precise 23.82 carat figure with no published method, a ring binding that fits nothing else in the record, Mormon circles with a motive to keep the object alive, the Cippus overlap, and a museum that has locked the book away for twenty three years without a single published test. Dylan closes on the ethic underneath all of it, that you correct your errors fast or nobody trusts the discovery you eventually make."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "The reason I can't stand this space over the last 15 years is nobody can be bothered to look at it.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "The forgeries sell way easier on the black market than to a real museum or institution who has more scrutiny.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Everything that is significant about the Etruscans is overlooked, and I think that's because there's this process called Greek mythological imperialism, which I cover ad nauseam.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "I can't just trust AI that it's truly a copy. It's useful as a tool to put me on the track of whether or not I should look into it further.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The amount of time that is invested to get this to you, just transliterating it alone took me a couple of weeks.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "If I was a betting man and I had a lot riding on this, I would bet fake.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "My favorite reason to bet against it is that Mormons are using it to make their own cult sound plausible. That's super scammy.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You don't want to ever get to a situation where you make a great discovery, but nobody takes you serious because your reputation is consistently being wrong.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "I'm really passionate about this, but I understand that I'm looking at a copy of a copy of a copy.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "I think we did a good deed for the historical record that has not been done in any kind of public accessible way.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
